title: Post-purchase onboarding: The 7-day sequence that saves the customers most businesses lose
hook: The seven days after a customer buys decide more than any ad you will run next month.
caption:
The seven days after a customer buys decide more than any ad you will run next month.

A business near 100k will often spend that window on a single welcome email and then go quiet for two weeks, then send a generic newsletter, then send a we miss you note after the customer is already gone.

Here is a different seven-day plan. Seven emails across one week that work for software, coaching, and small e-commerce.

Day zero is a welcome from a real person signed by a real name. One short paragraph that names the group the customer has joined and says what you will send them this week.

Day one points them at a small win. Give them one thing they can do in the product today that leaves them with something to show by the end of the day.

Day two shares a real story. Two or three sentences from another customer in that customer's own words, delivered as a quote, a screenshot, or a voice note.

Day three points them at a second use. This is the most important email in the set. A buyer who uses you for a second thing inside the first week tends to stay the longest.

Day four gives them a small setup that takes five minutes and saves them an hour later. A saved view, a template, a connection to a tool they already use.

Day five is a specific question. Ask what they tried this week that did not work. A specific question gets a specific answer, while a vague one gets silence.

Day seven proposes a standing time. Suggest a day of the week or a moment in their routine where using you fits naturally, so a purchase turns into a habit.

Seven emails across one week. It will not win a design award. It takes one afternoon to write properly, and it is the afternoon a business near 100k keeps putting off.

title: A 7-day onboarding teardown for businesses near 100k
hook: The seven days after a customer buys is the most valuable window you will ever have with them, and a business near 100k will often spend it on one welcome email and then go silent for two weeks.
tweets:
The seven days after a customer buys is the most valuable window you will ever have with them.

A business near 100k will often spend it on one welcome email and then go silent for two weeks.

Here is an email-by-email breakdown of what actually fits in those seven days.

Day zero goes out inside the first hour after the purchase.

One short paragraph from a real person signed by a real name. It names the group they have joined and says what you will send them this week. There is no tour and no checklist, only a greeting that reads like a human wrote it.

Day one points them at a small win.

Give them one thing they can do in the product today that ends with something to show by the end of the day. Skip the full feature tour, because a small finished step beats a long unfinished list every time.

Day two shares a real story.

Two or three sentences from another customer in that customer's own words, delivered as a quote, a screenshot, or a voice note. The rough version of a story is what gets read, while the polished case study is what gets skipped.

Day three points them at a second use.

This is the most important email in the set. A buyer who uses you for a second thing inside the first week stays the longest, and a buyer who misses this email is the one you will lose at month three.

Day four gives them a small setup that takes five minutes and saves them an hour later.

A saved view, a template named after them, a connection to a tool they already use. A small piece of their own work inside the product is what makes leaving feel expensive.

Day five is a specific question.

Ask what they tried this week that did not work, written in one line. A specific question gets a specific answer, while do you need help gets silence across every inbox that ever received it.

Day seven proposes a standing time.

Suggest a day of the week or a moment in their routine where using you fits naturally, such as a Tuesday after lunch or a Sunday evening. You are turning a one-time purchase into a weekly habit.

Seven emails across one week. It will not win a design award, and it takes one afternoon to write properly.

If that window is empty in your business right now, that is where this quarter's retention work actually lives.

title: The day zero email that predicts 30-day retention
hook: The first email after a customer buys has three jobs, and a business near 100k will often only do the first.
caption:
The first email after a customer buys has three jobs, and a business near 100k will often only do the first of them.

Here is a three-section template you can write in fifteen minutes.

Section one is the welcome. One sentence that names the group the buyer has joined, not the product they bought. Not welcome to the product, but welcome to the people who use it to do a specific thing in their week.

Section two is what to expect across the week. Three short lines that say what you will send, when it will land in their inbox, and what it will ask of them. The buyer now knows the shape of the week before it starts.

Section three is one small first step they can take today, followed by an invitation to reply if they want help. A reply from a real person inside one working day is the one thing that makes the reply rate climb.

Timing matters more than any line inside the email. Send it inside the first hour after the purchase, not twelve hours later and not the next morning. The customer is still in the moment of deciding they did the right thing, and you want to be there while they are.

title: LI Second Post: Retention does not show up next week
hook: Retention does not show up next week, and the first seven emails you send in the first seven days will change your business in roughly ninety days, not seven.
caption:
Retention does not show up next week.

The first seven emails you send across the seven days after a customer buys will change your business in roughly ninety days, not seven days.

A business near 100k will often try a new ad, a new feature, a new discount, and hope for a difference inside thirty days. When nothing moves in a month, the new thing gets dropped and replaced with the next one. Retention work does not show its face on that schedule.

Write the seven emails. Send them to every new customer from tomorrow. Do not touch them for three months. Then look at the ninety-day revenue and repeat-purchase numbers. That is the number retention speaks in.

title: How to read a competitor's ad like a creative strategist
hook: How to read one of your competitor's ads like a creative strategist. The move that changes your work more than any course on frameworks.
caption:
How to read one of your competitor's ads like a creative strategist.

Here is the move that changes your work more than any course on frameworks will. Pick one ad from a competitor you would like to work with and spend twenty minutes actually reading it, not scrolling past it and not just screenshotting it.

Four questions to run every time.

One. Who is the first line of this ad talking to. Picture the person, not the category. A specific person with an age, a life stage, and a mood. If you cannot picture them, the ad is not working as well as it looks and you have just noticed something real.

Two. What does the ad promise that person in the first three seconds. Not what the product is, the promise. Write it in one sentence.

Three. What did the brand do to make the promise believable. A face on camera, a before and after, a stat, a mechanism, a customer quote. Name the move out loud.

Four. What would you test next if you ran this account tomorrow. One specific change and your hypothesis on the result.

If you answer those four questions on four ads this week, your work gets sharper than any course could make it. You are training your eye to see what a creative strategist is paid to see.

title: How to tear down a winning ad (FB Page)
hook: How to tear down a winning ad when you are working toward becoming a seasoned creative strategist. Every creative strategist has a swipe file somewhere, and learning to actually look at an ad is what gets skipped.
caption:
How to tear down a winning ad when you are working toward becoming a seasoned creative strategist.

Every creative strategist has a swipe file somewhere on their laptop. Screenshots, bookmarks, a Notion page that gets long and never gets reread. The file is the easy part, while learning to actually look at an ad is what gets skipped.

Here are four questions that turn a swipe into a teardown. Run them on every ad you save for the next two weeks.

One. Who is this ad written for. Not the category, the specific person the first line is speaking to. Read the first line out loud, picture the person, and write one sentence about who that is, including age, life stage, and what they were doing when they saw this ad.

Two. What is the promise in the first three seconds. Not what the brand is selling, what the ad is saying it will give the viewer. Name it in one sentence.

Three. What did the brand do to make the promise believable. A face on camera, a before and after, a customer quote, a stat, a mechanism. Name the move out loud.

Four. What would you test next if you ran this account. Not what you would critique, what you would try. One specific change and your guess on what would happen.

If you answer those four questions on every ad you save, inside a month you will have a folder that reads like a strategy document. You will also find that your own hooks get easier to write.

A creative strategist is hired to answer question four for a living, so start practicing now.

title: CSOS IG Reel: Before you rewrite the copy, rewrite the buyer
hook: The ad is not landing, and before you rewrite a single word of the copy, read the first line out loud and picture the exact person it is talking to.
caption:

Read the first line out loud instead. Picture the exact person it is talking to, not the category and not the age bracket, a specific human with a mood and a day. If you cannot picture them, the ad was never going to land with a real buyer. The same words aimed at a clearer picture of who they are for will give you a completely different result by the end of the week.

Before you rewrite the copy, rewrite the buyer, and the copy starts writing itself.

Read the first line out loud and picture the exact person it is talking to, not the category and not the age range, a specific human with a day and a mood.
